title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (5 of 7)
hook: the whole method of yoga in two words, and Krishna said the same two words to Arjuna
tomorrow: Patanjali 1.13–1.14: practice, over a long time (6 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.1 and on: the five turnings. Right knowing, error, imagination, sleep, memory. Did a worry turn out to be imagination? Your line: now. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

Remember Arjuna in the Gita, a few months ago on this path? Somewhere in the sixth chapter he stops Krishna and says, more or less: this is all beautiful, but my mind is restless. Holding it still is like holding the wind. Anyone who has tried to meditate for five minutes knows the feeling. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees: yes, the mind is hard to hold. And then he gives two words for how it's done. Patanjali, in thread twelve, gives the very same two.
screen: `ARJUNA: MY MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Thread twelve: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. By practice and non-attachment, they are stilled. They, meaning the turnings. Two words carry the whole method. Abhyasa, practice: coming back, again and again, to the thing you've chosen. Vairagya, non-attachment: letting go of the pull. Literally it means without coloring, without the red flower staining the crystal. Teachers often say the two are like the two wings of a bird. One wing alone, and you fly in circles. Practice without letting go becomes grinding: you sit every day, jaw clenched, demanding results. Letting go without practice becomes drifting: you're very relaxed and nothing changes. You need both. Coming back, and not clutching. And here is the Gita's answer to Arjuna, in the sixth chapter: the mind is restless, hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by dispassion. The same pair, in the same order. Two great texts, from different schools, agree on the method. Now make it small. Practice is the phone you put face down again. Non-attachment is not caring, for a moment, whether it buzzes. Practice is returning to the breath. Non-attachment is not needing the breath to feel special. Tomorrow and the day after, Patanjali takes each wing on its own. Today, just notice that you need two.
screen: `ABHYĀSA-VAIRĀGYĀBHYĀṀ TAN-NIRODHAḤ.` · `ABHYASA: COMING BACK, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `VAIRAGYA: LETTING GO OF THE PULL.` · `TWO WINGS OF ONE BIRD.` · then, large: `PRACTICE, AND LET GO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose one thing to return to: the breath at the nose, or a word, or the sound of the room. That's the first wing. When the mind wanders, and it will, come back. Don't scold it. That's the second wing: no clutching, no scorekeeping. Come back, let go, come back, let go. The rhythm of it is the whole method, small. If you pray, the thing you return to can be a name of God. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and thread twelve: by practice and non-attachment, the turnings are stilled. Abhyasa and vairagya. Two wings.
Your line: now. Today, pick one small thing to come back to every time you get distracted, and let go of how well you're doing it. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers of meditation often pair abhyasa and vairagya, citing both Yoga Sutra 1.12 and Bhagavad Gita 6.35, and describe daily practice as returning again and again without clinging to results.

options: you're wrong, the mind is easy to hold.
yes, it's hard: practice and dispassion hold it.

fork.reveal: he agrees the mind is restless, and gives two words: practice and dispassion. Patanjali's thread twelve names the same pair.

original.note: Sanskrit: abhyasa, repeated practice + vairagya, non-attachment (vi + raga: without coloring or passion).

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation is about trying harder.
what it means: two wings: practice, coming back again and again, and non-attachment, letting go of the pull.
what a scholar hears: vairagya from vi-raga, 'without coloring or passion'; Gita 6.35 uses the same pair, abhyasa and vairagya, in answer to Arjuna.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.34–6.35 (the mind like the wind; held by practice and dispassion)

notes: The 'two wings of a bird' image is a common teaching simile, not in the sutra; presented as 'teachers often say'.
Arjuna's line (6.34) compares holding the mind to holding the wind; paraphrased. Gita 6.35 abhyasa and vairagya: confirm the Gita's exact terms (abhyasena ... vairagyena).
'A few months ago on this path': Camp 4 (the Gita) ran days 157–231; confirm the chapter-six days fell there.
